headline: Google applies Gemini 4 Argon to robotics, cites 87% score
dek: DeepMind shows the model directing real and simulated robots and says it beats other frontier models on ERQA.

s2.label: What happened
s2.title: 87% on a physical-reasoning test
body: Google DeepMind says Gemini 4 Argon scored 87% on ERQA, a test of physical reasoning in 3D environments, beating every other frontier model (Google DeepMind).
It describes Argon as a general-purpose physical reasoning model, usable from planning to direct robot control (Google DeepMind).

s3.label: How it works
s3.title: What the model did with robots
s3.body: According to Google, the demos used real and simulated robots, across four areas.

points.t: It built a digital twin of the bin and rehearsed the motion before moving the real robot (Google DeepMind).
It watched a person do a task and mapped the hand motion to a 76-degree humanoid (Google DeepMind).
It found the odd ball among 12 in three weighings, using only cameras (Google DeepMind).

s4.label: Why it matters
s4.title: Synthetic data to train robots
body: From a single tabletop photo, Argon built a calibrated simulation and produced over 4,500 training episodes (Google DeepMind).
Google says that training lifted a real robot's success rate from 56% to 75% and cut completion time from 35 to 24 seconds.

stat.cap: real robot success rate after the training

items.t: DeepMind says one model can support most stages of building and testing a robot (Google DeepMind).
In a 136-second origami fold, it labeled each stage and flagged mistakes (Google DeepMind).
The results come from the company's own demos and the ERQA benchmark (Google DeepMind).

caption.hook: Google DeepMind says Gemini 4 Argon scored 87% on ERQA, a physical-reasoning test for robots.
body: According to the company, the model beats every other frontier model on the benchmark. In demos, it controlled a Spot robot, mapped a human video onto a humanoid and found the odd ball among 12 in three weighings.

Google also says Argon generated over 4,500 simulated episodes from one photo, lifting a real robot's success rate from 56% to 75%. The results come from DeepMind's own blog post. DeepMind says one model could support most stages of building and testing a robot.
